In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

BPA is an effective a posteriori method for analyzing the host context of speciation in parasites, and reconciliation methods, including the most recent modifications of basic reconciliation methods embodied in TreeMap 2.0, are effective a priori methods for testing the fit of parasite phylogenies against a known host phylogenetic tree.
BPA and TreeMap 2 represent the most sophisticated methods currently available for the study of cospeciation in host‐parasite associations.
BPA and reconciled tree analysis, although they both use the same null hypothesis, are designed to address different questions, and they are therefore fundamentally different methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

BPA, when applied to host–parasites systems in which host‐specific parasites are the only parasites considered, is a more parsimonious method than reconciliation methods for summarizing complex histories.

the a priori assumptions of reconciliation methods, which are designed to fit the data to a null hypothesis, are more parsimonious than the a posteriori assumptions of BPA, which are designed for explanatory power.
BPA, as an a posterioric method, is more robust and flexible than a priori reconciliation methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reconciliation method is not a single method but a class of methods that can be modified to implement different research strategies.
BPA is an important tool for comparative studies of cospeciation and host–parasitism, but it is not the only tool.

the a priori assumptions and a posteriori explanatory tools of different methods should be made explicit, so as to avoid confusion about the results of comparative analyses of host–par asite associations.
